q: A mixture that has the same composition throughout, such as salt dissolved in water, is...
e: Uniform throughout means homogeneous.

q: Which is a heterogeneous mixture?
e: The parts of trail mix can be seen and separated.

q: Which is a pure substance that is a compound?
e: Water is a pure substance made of two elements bonded.

q: A sample contains only one kind of atom. It is...
e: Elements contain just one type of atom.

q: A student models a substance as two different kinds of atoms bonded in a fixed ratio. What is it?
e: Fixed-ratio bonded atoms of different elements form a compound.

q: Which of these is a homogeneous mixture?
o: a pile of sand and iron filings
e: Vinegar looks the same throughout.

q: How does a mixture differ from a compound?
o: a compound can be separated by filtering
a mixture is a pure substance
the parts of a mixture are not chemically bonded
a mixture always has a fixed formula
e: Mixtures keep the properties of their parts.

q: Elements on the periodic table are arranged by increasing...
o: state of matter at room temperature
e: Atomic number is the number of protons.

q: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, which elements are the reactants made of?
e: H is hydrogen and O is oxygen.

q: Which group on the periodic table contains elements that rarely react?
e: Their outer shells are full.

q: Sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl) react to form NaCl. Which tool tells you what the symbols stand for?
e: It lists each element and its symbol.

q: In the reaction CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, which atoms are involved?
e: The symbols C, H and O appear.

q: Elements in the same column of the periodic table tend to have...
e: They have the same number of outer electrons.

q: In the periodic table, metals are generally found...
e: Nonmetals are on the right.

q: Water molecules sticking to each other is called...
e: Cohesion is attraction between like molecules.

q: Water molecules sticking to other surfaces, like glass, is called...
e: Adhesion is attraction between unlike substances.

q: Why do small drops of water form beads on a waxy leaf?
e: Cohesion and surface tension hold the drop together.

q: A water strider can walk on water because of...
o: low density of the strider only
e: The surface behaves like a thin skin.

q: Water travels up through plant roots, stems and leaves partly because of...
e: Water sticks to itself and to the vessel walls.

q: A paper towel soaks up spilled water because water molecules...
o: adhere to the fibers and pull other molecules along
e: Adhesion plus cohesion draws water upward.

q: Which observation is caused by surface tension?
o: a drop of water forming a rounded dome on a coin
e: Surface tension pulls the surface into a tight shape.

q: A solution with a pH of 2 is...
e: pH below 7 is acidic.

q: Pure water has a pH of about...
e: Pure water is neutral.

q: Which pH value is most basic?
e: Higher pH means a stronger base.

q: Which property is common to bases?
e: Bases feel slippery (like soap).

q: Lemon juice has a pH of 2 and baking soda solution has a pH of 9. Which statement is correct?
o: lemon juice is more acidic than water, and the baking soda solution is basic
e: Below 7 is acid, above 7 is base.

q: What happens to pH when a base is added to an acid?
o: the pH stays exactly the same
e: Neutralization moves toward neutral.

q: How many times more acidic is a solution of pH 3 than one of pH 4?
e: Each pH step is a factor of 10.

q: The law of conservation of mass says that in a chemical reaction, mass is...
e: Total mass stays the same.

q: 10 g of reactant A reacts completely with 15 g of reactant B. What is the total mass of the products?
e: Mass of products equals mass of reactants.

q: A chemical equation is balanced when...
o: each type of atom has the same count on both sides
e: Atoms are only rearranged.

q: Is the equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O balanced?
o: no, there are more H on the right
yes, but only the O is balanced
no, there are more O on the right
yes, 4 H and 2 O on each side
e: Count: 4 H and 2 O on both sides.

q: Is the equation H2 + O2 -> H2O balanced?
o: no, there are 2 O on the left and 1 on the right
no, there are more H on the right
e: Oxygen atoms are not equal.

q: A student burns a candle in an open room and the candle seems to lose mass. Where did the mass go?
o: into gases like carbon dioxide and water vapor released into the air
e: Mass is conserved when all products are counted.

q: Balance: N2 + __H2 -> 2NH3. What number goes in the blank?
e: 6 H atoms are needed on the right so 3 H2.

q: Newton's Second Law can be written as...
e: Force equals mass times acceleration.

q: A 2 kg cart is pushed with a net force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
If the net force on an object is made twice as large and the mass stays the same, the acceleration...
e: Acceleration is proportional to force.

q: If the mass of an object doubles and the force stays the same, the acceleration...
e: Acceleration is inversely related to mass.

q: What net force gives a 4 kg object an acceleration of 3 m/s2?
A 1,000 kg car accelerates at 2 m/s2. What is the net force on the car?
Two carts get the same push. Cart A has a mass of 1 kg and Cart B has a mass of 3 kg. Which accelerates more?
e: Less mass means more acceleration.

q: A seat belt keeps a passenger in place during a sudden stop. This mostly demonstrates Newton's...
e: The passenger's body tends to keep moving.

q: A swimmer pushes water backward and moves forward. This demonstrates Newton's...
e: Action and reaction forces.

q: A bigger force on a shopping cart makes it speed up more. This demonstrates Newton's...
e: More force gives more acceleration.

q: A car hits a wall. Which laws help explain why an unrestrained passenger is injured?
o: First Law (inertia) and Second Law (large force over a short time)
e: Inertia keeps the passenger moving; stopping quickly takes a large force.

q: On a roller coaster, riders feel pressed into their seats on a sharp turn. Which idea explains this?
o: inertia: their bodies tend to keep moving in a straight line
e: The seat pushes inward to change their direction.

q: A football player tackles another. Which statement is correct?
o: the lighter player exerts more force
each player exerts an equal and opposite force on the other
e: Third Law pairs are equal and opposite.

q: Airbags in cars reduce injury by...
o: increasing the time over which the passenger stops, so the force is smaller
increasing the speed of the car
e: Same change in motion over longer time means less force.

q: The height of a wave from its rest position to its crest is its...
e: Greater amplitude means more energy.

q: Frequency is the number of waves that pass a point per...
e: Measured in hertz.

q: Which electromagnetic wave has the longest wavelength?
e: Radio waves are at the long-wavelength end.

q: As the frequency of an electromagnetic wave increases, its wavelength...
e: In a given medium, wavelength and frequency are inversely related.

q: Which has the highest frequency?
e: Gamma rays are at the high-energy end.

q: Which color of visible light has the shortest wavelength?
e: Violet is at the short end.

q: Which type of electromagnetic wave is used in radiation therapy to kill cancer cells?
e: High-energy rays can damage cells.

q: Microwave ovens heat food using...
e: Microwaves make water molecules vibrate.

q: Wi-Fi and cell phones send information using...
e: These waves carry signals without wires.

q: Fiber optic cables transmit information using...
e: Light bounces along glass strands.

q: Ultraviolet light is used to sterilize equipment because it...
o: can damage the DNA of germs
e: UV breaks down microbes.

q: Why should people wear sunscreen?
o: to protect skin from harmful ultraviolet rays
e: UV can cause sunburn and skin damage.

q: A doctor uses X-rays to see a broken bone because X-rays...
o: are absorbed by all tissue equally
pass through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone
pass through bone but not skin
e: Bone absorbs more.

q: Stars form from clouds of gas and dust called...
e: Gravity pulls the nebula together.

q: What happens when a star the size of our Sun runs out of fuel?
o: it becomes a red giant, then a white dwarf
e: Medium-mass stars end as white dwarfs.

q: A very massive star ends its life as a(n)...
e: It explodes and may leave a neutron star or black hole.

q: On the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, most stars (like the Sun) fall in the...
e: A diagonal band includes most stars.

q: On an H-R diagram, which stars are hot but dim?
e: They are small, so dim despite high temperature.

q: A star is cool but very bright. On the H-R diagram it is most likely a...
e: Large surface area makes it bright.

q: The Sun produces energy by...
e: Nuclear fusion releases energy.

q: Our solar system is located in the...
e: The Milky Way is our home galaxy.

q: A galaxy with arms that wind around a bright center is a...
e: Spiral galaxies have arms.

q: A galaxy shaped like a smooth oval with no clear arms is...
e: Smooth shape means elliptical.

q: A galaxy with no regular shape is...
e: Irregular galaxies lack a defined structure.

q: The Milky Way is classified as a...
e: It has spiral arms.

q: Where is our solar system located in the Milky Way?
o: in one of the spiral arms, far from the center
e: We are in the Orion Arm region.

q: Galaxies are held together by...
e: Gravity binds stars and gas.

q: Which theory describes the origin of the universe from a hot, dense beginning?
e: The universe has been expanding since.

q: Galaxies are moving away from each other. This is evidence that the universe is...
e: Redshift shows galaxies receding.

q: Light from distant galaxies is shifted toward the red end of the spectrum. This is called...
e: It shows the galaxies move away.

q: Cosmic microwave background radiation is evidence for...
o: the early hot universe after the Big Bang
e: It is leftover radiation from early times.

q: Why do scientists look at light from distant galaxies to study the early universe?
o: light takes a long time to travel, so we see the galaxy as it was long ago
e: Looking far away is looking back in time.

q: A scientific theory is best described as...
o: an explanation supported by a large body of evidence
e: Theories are tested and supported repeatedly.

q: Which evidence supports the Big Bang theory?
o: the observed expansion of the universe
e: Expansion implies a beginning.

q: What is the main energy source for Earth's weather?
e: The Sun heats the air and water unevenly.

q: Differences in heating between land and sea cause...
e: Warm air rises and cooler air moves in.

q: Water evaporating from the ocean adds what to the atmosphere?
e: Water vapor condenses into clouds.

q: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere over a short time. Climate is...
o: the average weather in a region over a long time
e: Climate is long-term.

q: Which process transfers energy from the ocean to the atmosphere?
e: Evaporation carries energy in water vapor.

q: A region near the equator is warmer than one near the poles because...
o: sunlight strikes more directly at the equator
the equator is closer to the Moon
e: Direct rays are more concentrated.

q: Winds are caused by differences in...
e: Air flows from high to low pressure.

q: The Coriolis effect is caused by...
e: It curves moving air and water.

q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis effect deflects moving air to the...
e: Winds curve clockwise-ish to the right.

q: Most of the United States is in a belt of winds that blow mostly from the west. They are called the...
e: Weather systems usually move west to east.

q: Why do weather systems in Texas usually move from west to east?
e: The global wind belt pushes them east.

q: The jet stream is...
o: a fast current of air high in the atmosphere
e: It steers weather systems.

q: Warm moist air rising at the equator is part of a global pattern called...
e: Heat drives the movement of air around Earth.

q: Hurricanes form over...
e: They draw energy from warm water.

q: What sea surface temperature is generally needed for hurricanes to form?
e: Warm water supplies heat and moisture.

q: A hurricane weakens when it moves over land because it loses...
o: its supply of warm, moist ocean air
e: Land cuts off the energy source.

q: In the Northern Hemisphere, a hurricane spins...
e: Because of the Coriolis effect.

q: The calm center of a hurricane is called the...
e: Winds are light in the eye.

q: Storm surge is dangerous because it...
o: pushes a wall of seawater onto land
e: Surge floods coastal areas.

q: Warm ocean currents like the Gulf Stream can affect hurricanes by...
o: supplying warm water that feeds storms
e: Warm water adds energy.

q: A large volcanic eruption can cool Earth's climate temporarily because ash and gases...
e: Particles in the air block some sunlight.

q: A large meteor impact could change climate by throwing dust into the atmosphere that...
e: Darker, cooler conditions could follow.

q: A sudden change in a major ocean current, such as the Gulf Stream, could...
e: Currents move heat.

q: Volcanoes release carbon dioxide. Over millions of years this can...
e: CO2 is a greenhouse gas.

q: Which natural event can quickly cool Earth for a year or two?
e: Sulfur aerosols reflect sunlight.

q: Ice cores show gas bubbles from long ago. Scientists use them to study...
e: Trapped air shows ancient atmosphere.

q: The release of methane from thawing permafrost could...
e: Methane is a greenhouse gas.

q: Burning fossil fuels adds which greenhouse gas to the air?
e: Burning carbon fuels makes CO2.

q: Cutting down forests can raise CO2 levels because fewer trees remain to...
e: Trees take in CO2 for photosynthesis.

q: Cities are often warmer than nearby rural areas. This is called the...
e: Pavement and buildings hold heat.

q: Which human activity adds methane to the atmosphere?
e: These practices release methane.

q: Which action would help reduce greenhouse gas emissions?
o: switching from coal to wind and solar power
e: Renewables release little CO2.

q: Scientific measurements show atmospheric CO2 has risen since the Industrial Revolution. The best explanation is...
e: The rise tracks human fuel use.

q: Urbanization affects climate mainly by...
o: replacing vegetation with surfaces that absorb heat
e: Pavement and rooftops warm the area.

q: Plants take in carbon dioxide during...
e: They use CO2 to make sugars.

q: Where is carbon stored for millions of years?
e: Dead organisms and shells became fuels and rock.

q: When wood burns, carbon returns to the air as...
e: Combustion releases CO2.

q: The oceans take up CO2 from the air. This helps to...
o: slow the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere
increase the CO2 in the air
e: Oceans act as a carbon sink.

q: Which sequence correctly shows carbon moving through a food chain?
o: air to plant to animal to decomposers to air
animal to plant to air only
e: Carbon flows through organisms and back to the atmosphere.

q: Decomposers help the carbon cycle by...
o: breaking down dead matter and releasing CO2
e: Carbon is recycled.

q: If a disease kills most of the rabbits in a food web, the foxes that eat rabbits will most likely...
e: Fewer prey means less energy for predators.

q: A wildfire destroys many plants in a forest. What happens to the herbivores?
o: they lose food and their numbers fall
e: Less producer energy.

q: Removing wolves from an ecosystem can cause the deer population to...
e: No predator limits the deer.

q: An invasive species eats a native insect that many birds eat. What is the likely effect on the birds?
o: less food, so bird populations may decline
e: Energy transfer to birds is reduced.

q: A keystone species is one that...
o: has a large effect on its ecosystem relative to its numbers
e: Removing it can disrupt the whole web.

q: A factory pollutes a lake and kills the algae. Which organisms are affected first?
e: The base of the food web is disrupted.

q: How does a drought affect the transfer of energy in a food web?
o: less plant growth means less energy for consumers
e: Producers capture less energy.

q: Succession that begins on bare rock where no soil exists is called...
e: Soil must form first.

q: Succession after a forest fire, where soil is still present, is called...
e: Soil remains, so recovery is faster.

q: Which organisms are usually the first to colonize bare rock?
e: They break rock down and help form soil.

q: A volcano creates new land from lava. The first stage of life that appears is...
e: Pioneer species begin soil formation.

q: As succession proceeds, species diversity typically...
e: More niches become available.

q: After a farm field is abandoned, grasses are followed by shrubs and then trees. This is an example of...
e: The soil was already present.

q: Why is secondary succession usually faster than primary succession?
o: soil and seeds are already present
there is no sunlight in primary
e: Soil formation takes a long time.

q: Biodiversity refers to...
o: the variety of living things in an area
e: More species means higher biodiversity.

q: An ecosystem with high biodiversity is usually more...
e: Many species can fill roles if one declines.

q: A farm with only one crop is at risk because...
o: one disease could destroy the entire crop
e: Low diversity increases vulnerability.

q: Why does biodiversity help an ecosystem recover after a disturbance?
o: different species fill different roles and help rebuild
e: Redundancy provides resilience.

q: A coral reef with many species is healthier than one with few because...
o: species depend on each other in many ways
e: Complex interactions maintain balance.

q: Which activity reduces biodiversity?
e: Habitat loss is the leading cause.

q: Why is protecting many species important for people?
o: ecosystems provide food, clean air, clean water and medicines
e: Humans depend on healthy ecosystems.

q: Which cell part controls the cell's activities and holds the DNA?
e: The nucleus is the control center.

q: Which organelle releases energy from food for the cell?
e: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration.

q: Which organelle captures light energy to make sugar?
e: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells.

q: Which structure gives a plant cell its rigid shape?
e: The cell wall surrounds the membrane.

q: Ribosomes in a cell function to...
e: Ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins.

q: Which part of a cell regulates what enters and leaves?
e: It is selectively permeable.

q: Which cell part is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
e: Plants perform photosynthesis.

q: Genes are located on...
e: Chromosomes carry many genes.

q: A gene is a segment of DNA that determines a(n)...
e: Genes code for traits.

q: Offspring receive genetic information from...
e: Each parent gives half.

q: Humans have 46 chromosomes in body cells. How many does an egg cell have?
e: Sex cells carry half the number.

q: Different forms of a gene are called...
e: Alleles can be dominant or recessive.

q: A trait that shows up when only one dominant allele is present is a...
e: A dominant allele masks a recessive one.

q: In a Punnett square of Bb x Bb (B dominant), what fraction of offspring are bb?
e: One of four boxes is bb.

q: A physical feature that helps an organism survive is called a(n)...
e: Examples: fur, claws, beaks.

q: Birds migrating south for winter is an example of a...
e: It is an action that helps survival.

q: A camel storing fat in its hump to survive long periods without food is a...
e: It relates to body processes.

q: Why are individuals with helpful adaptations more likely to pass on their genes?
o: they mate more often by design
they are more likely to survive and reproduce
e: Natural selection favors them.

q: A population has some individuals with thick fur and some with thin fur. A cold winter occurs. What is likely to happen?
o: those with thick fur survive more often
e: The environment favors thick fur.

q: Octopuses changing color to blend in is an example of a(n)...
e: Camouflage increases survival.

q: Which would help a polar bear survive in the Arctic?
o: a thick layer of fat and white fur
a long thin tail for gliding
e: Insulation and camouflage.
